# Loading the data

## Reading the files

Two practical pitfalls are handled here:

* **Column type guessing.** `read_csv()` guesses each column's type from the
  first 1 000 rows by default. Many NHANES variables are empty for the first
  1 000 participants (e.g. variables measured only in a subsample), so a column
  can be guessed wrongly and its later values silently turned into `NA`. We
  therefore let readr look at all rows (`guess_max`).
* **Encoding of the codebook.** The codebook is not UTF-8 but Windows-1252
  (it contains typographic apostrophes and the `µ` sign); reading it with the
  default encoding fails or garbles the labels.

```{r load}
nhanes_raw <- load_raw_data()    # defined in R/utils.R: read_csv() with guess_max = 20000
codebook   <- load_codebook()    # defined in R/utils.R: Windows-1252 encoding
```

What would have gone wrong with the default `guess_max`? We read the file a
second time with default settings and compare how many values are present in
each column.

```{r guess-max-check}
nhanes_default <- read_csv(paths$raw_data, show_col_types = FALSE)   # readr defaults
values_lost <- tibble(
  variable      = names(nhanes_raw),
  present_full  = colSums(!is.na(nhanes_raw)),
  present_guess = colSums(!is.na(nhanes_default))
) %>%
  filter(present_full != present_guess)

nrow(values_lost)   # number of columns that would have lost values
values_lost
rm(nhanes_default)
```

## Basic integrity checks

```{r integrity}
dim(nhanes_raw)                                     # participants x variables

# Is SEQN a unique participant identifier (one row = one person)?
n_distinct(nhanes_raw$SEQN) == nrow(nhanes_raw)

# Do data and codebook describe exactly the same variables, in the same order?
setequal(names(nhanes_raw), codebook$variable)
identical(names(nhanes_raw), codebook$variable)

# How were the columns read?
table(map_chr(nhanes_raw, ~ class(.x)[1]))
names(nhanes_raw)[map_lgl(nhanes_raw, is.character)]  # the only non-numeric column(s)

# Completely empty variables (read as "logical" because there is nothing to guess from)
names(nhanes_raw)[colSums(!is.na(nhanes_raw)) == 0]
```

# What kinds of variables are there?

The 486 columns are not all "features". Using the codebook we give every
variable a **role**:

* `identifier`: SEQN.
* `survey design / weight`: sampling weights (`WT...`) and design variables
  (strata, PSU, release cycle). They describe how participants were sampled,
  not the participants themselves.
* `comment code`: flags belonging to another variable, mostly "value was below
  the limit of detection" (see section 6).
* `unit duplicate`: the same measurement reported a second time in another unit
  (e.g. cholesterol in mg/dL **and** mmol/L). Detected as two variables in the
  same data file whose labels are identical apart from the unit in brackets.
* `measurement`: everything else, i.e. the actual candidate features.

```{r variable-roles}
n_distinct_values <- map_int(nhanes_raw, ~ n_distinct(.x, na.rm = TRUE))
pct_missing_all   <- colMeans(is.na(nhanes_raw)) * 100

var_info <- codebook %>%
  mutate(
    position    = row_number(),
    n_distinct  = n_distinct_values[variable],
    pct_missing = pct_missing_all[variable],
    # label without a trailing "(unit)", used to find unit duplicates
    base_label  = str_trim(str_remove(label, "\\s*\\([^()]*\\)\\s*$")),
    role = case_when(
      variable == "SEQN" ~ "identifier",
      str_detect(variable, "^WT") |
        variable %in% c("SDDSRVYR", "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU") ~ "survey design / weight",
      str_detect(label, regex("comment|cmt|comt", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "comment code",
      TRUE ~ "measurement"
    )
  ) %>%
  # second (and later) variable with the same base label in the same file =
  # unit duplicate. FASTQX_L is excluded: there "(hours)" and "(minutes)" are
  # two halves of one duration, not duplicates.
  group_by(file, base_label, role) %>%
  mutate(role = if_else(role == "measurement" & file != "FASTQX_L" & row_number() > 1,
                        "unit duplicate", role)) %>%
  ungroup()

count(var_info, role)
```

The unit duplicates that were detected (checked numerically in section 9):

```{r unit-duplicates}
var_info %>% filter(role == "unit duplicate") %>% select(variable, label, file) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

For the measurement variables we also make a first, **heuristic** guess of the
data type from the number of distinct values. This is only a starting point:
whether a coded variable is nominal or ordinal (e.g. education level) must be
checked in the NHANES documentation for each variable that we end up using.

```{r variable-types}
var_info <- var_info %>%
  mutate(type_guess = case_when(
    role != "measurement" ~ NA_character_,
    n_distinct <= 2       ~ "binary",
    n_distinct <= 15      ~ "categorical / coded",
    TRUE                  ~ "continuous / count"
  ))

var_info %>% filter(role == "measurement") %>%
  count(component, type_guess) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = type_guess, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r fig-variable-roles, fig.height = 8}
ggplot(var_info, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_inorder(file)), fill = role)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_grid(component ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = okabe_ito) +
  labs(x = "number of variables", y = "NHANES data file", fill = "role",
       title = "Composition of the merged file: only part of the 486 columns are features") +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0), legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Who is in the data?

```{r participants}
participants <- nhanes_raw %>%
  transmute(
    SEQN,
    age    = RIDAGEYR,
    sex    = factor(RIAGENDR, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    status = factor(RIDSTATR, levels = 1:2,
                    labels = c("Interview only", "Interview + examination")),
    ethnicity = factor(RIDRETH3, levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7),
                       labels = c("Mexican American", "Other Hispanic",
                                  "Non-Hispanic White", "Non-Hispanic Black",
                                  "Non-Hispanic Asian", "Other / multiracial")),
    group = case_when(
      RIDSTATR == 1  ~ "Interview only",
      RIDAGEYR < 20  ~ "Examined, < 20 y",
      TRUE           ~ "Examined, \u2265 20 y"
    ) %>% factor(levels = c("Interview only", "Examined, < 20 y", "Examined, \u2265 20 y"))
  )

count(participants, status)
count(participants, group)
count(participants, sex)
sum(participants$age == 80)   # participants at the age cap
```

ggplot(participants, aes(y = fct_rev(fct_infreq(ethnicity)))) +
  geom_bar(fill = okabe_ito[4]) +
  geom_text(aes(label = after_stat(count)), stat = "count", hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2) +

# Missing data

## How much is missing per variable?

```{r fig-missing-per-variable}
pct_interview_only <- 100 * mean(nhanes_raw$RIDSTATR == 1)

var_info %>%
  filter(role == "measurement") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(variable, pct_missing), y = pct_missing, colour = component)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pct_interview_only, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = pct_interview_only + 4, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           label = sprintf("%.1f %% of participants were never examined", pct_interview_only)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = okabe_ito) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "measurement variables, sorted by % missing", y = "% missing",
       title = "No lab or exam variable can be less incomplete than the share of non-examined participants") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Is missingness random, or caused by the study design?

If values were missing completely at random (MCAR), the percentage missing
would be similar in every group of participants. Here we compare three groups
defined by the design: not examined, examined children/teenagers, examined
adults. Each tile is the average % missing over all measurement variables of
one data file.

```{r missing-by-group}
measurement_vars <- var_info %>% filter(role == "measurement") %>% pull(variable)

missing_by_group <- nhanes_raw %>%
  mutate(group = participants$group) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(measurement_vars), ~ 100 * mean(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-group, names_to = "variable", values_to = "pct_missing") %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, file, component), by = "variable") %>%
  group_by(group, component, file) %>%
  summarise(pct_missing = mean(pct_missing), .groups = "drop")
```

```{r fig-missing-by-group, fig.height = 9}
ggplot(missing_by_group, aes(x = group, y = fct_rev(fct_inorder(file)), fill = pct_missing)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct_missing)), size = 3) +
  facet_grid(component ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = okabe_ito[6], limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NHANES data file", fill = "% missing",
       title = "Missingness depends on who was examined and on their age: it is not MCAR") +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))
```

## Missingness pattern at the participant level

A random subset of 400 participants (rows, sorted by age within each group) by
all measurement variables (columns, in codebook order). Vertical blocks of
missing values that start and stop at file boundaries show that whole lab
panels are either measured or not (subsamples).

```{r fig-missing-matrix, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 11}
subset_ids <- participants %>% slice_sample(n = 400) %>% arrange(group, age) %>%
  mutate(row = row_number())

nhanes_raw %>%
  filter(SEQN %in% subset_ids$SEQN) %>%
  select(SEQN, all_of(measurement_vars)) %>%
  mutate(across(-SEQN, is.na)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-SEQN, names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing") %>%
  left_join(select(subset_ids, SEQN, row, group), by = "SEQN") %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, position, component), by = "variable") %>%
  mutate(column = dense_rank(position)) %>%   # consecutive columns, no gaps
  ggplot(aes(x = column, y = row, fill = missing)) +
  geom_raster() +
  facet_grid(group ~ component, scales = "free", space = "free",
             labeller = labeller(component = c(Demographics = "Demo", Examination = "Exam",
                                               Laboratory = "Laboratory",
                                               Questionnaire = "Questionnaire"))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey85", `TRUE` = "black"),
                    labels = c("present", "missing")) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = "variables (codebook order)", y = "participants (sorted by age)", fill = NULL,
       title = "Missingness comes in blocks: whole lab panels are measured or not") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0), legend.position = "bottom")
```

# Values that are not real measurements

## Codes for "refused" and "don't know"

NHANES stores answers such as *refused* and *don't know* as numbers
(typically 7/9, 77/99, 777/999, ...) instead of `NA`. `is.na()` does not see
them, and a mean or regression would treat them as real values.

Detection rule (heuristic): for every questionnaire, demographic and fasting
variable, a value from {7, 9, 77, 99, 777, 999, ...} is flagged when it is
**larger than every other value of that variable, with a gap** (more than 1
above the largest regular value). This catches e.g. the 9 in education
(regular values 1–5) but not a real answer of 7 drinks per day, nor real
categories that simply continue the scale, such as code 7 "other race /
multiracial" in RIDRETH3 (values 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7) or "7 or more people" in
household size (1–7). Every
flagged variable must still be checked against the NHANES documentation.

```{r special-codes}
code_values <- c(7, 9, 77, 99, 777, 999, 7777, 9999, 77777, 99999, 777777, 999999)

scan_vars <- var_info %>%
  filter(role == "measurement",
         component %in% c("Demographics", "Questionnaire") | file == "FASTQX_L") %>%
  pull(variable)

find_special_codes <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (!is.numeric(x)) return(NULL)
  regular <- x[!x %in% code_values]
  if (length(regular) == 0) return(NULL)
  suspects <- x[x %in% code_values & x > max(regular) + 1]
  if (length(suspects) == 0) return(NULL)
  count(tibble(code = suspects), code)
}

special_codes <- map(set_names(scan_vars), ~ find_special_codes(nhanes_raw[[.x]])) %>%
  compact() %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "variable") %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  relocate(label, .after = variable)

knitr::kable(special_codes)
```

## Capped (top-coded) values

Some continuous variables are capped for privacy reasons: everybody above the
cap gets the cap value. This shows up as a spike at the maximum.

```{r fig-top-coding, fig.height = 3.5}
p_age <- ggplot(nhanes_raw, aes(RIDAGEYR)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = okabe_ito[2]) +
  labs(x = "age (RIDAGEYR), cap = 80", y = "participants")
p_pir <- ggplot(filter(nhanes_raw, !is.na(INDFMPIR)), aes(INDFMPIR)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = okabe_ito[2]) +
  labs(x = "income-to-poverty ratio (INDFMPIR), cap = 5", y = "participants")
p_age + p_pir + plot_annotation(title = "Top-coded variables: a spike at the maximum value")
```

```{r top-coding-counts}
c(age_80 = sum(nhanes_raw$RIDAGEYR == 80),
  income_ratio_5 = sum(nhanes_raw$INDFMPIR == 5, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Values below the limit of detection (LOD)

For many lab tests a comment code tells whether the value was **below the
limit of detection** (code 1) or not (code 0). For those results NHANES does
not store the (unknown) true value but a fixed substitute (LOD / √2). Each
comment code is linked to the measurement it belongs to (the nearest preceding
measurement variable in the same file).

```{r lod}
measurement_positions <- var_info %>% filter(role == "measurement") %>%
  select(position, file, variable)

lod_info <- var_info %>%
  filter(role == "comment code", component == "Laboratory") %>%
  select(comment_variable = variable, position, file) %>%
  mutate(variable = map2_chr(position, file, function(p, f) {
    measurement_positions %>% filter(file == f, position < p) %>%
      slice_max(position, n = 1) %>% pull(variable)
  })) %>%
  mutate(
    n_measured    = map_int(comment_variable, ~ sum(!is.na(nhanes_raw[[.x]]))),
    pct_below_lod = map_dbl(comment_variable, ~ 100 * mean(nhanes_raw[[.x]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
  ) %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, label), by = "variable")

# sanity check: comment codes only contain 0 / 1
map(lod_info$comment_variable, ~ unique(na.omit(nhanes_raw[[.x]]))) %>% unlist() %>% unique()

summarise(lod_info,
          n_lab_tests_with_lod_flag = n(),
          more_than_half_below_lod  = sum(pct_below_lod > 50))
```

```{r fig-lod, fig.height = 13}
lod_info %>%
  filter(pct_below_lod > 0) %>%
  mutate(label = str_trunc(label, 45)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_below_lod, y = fct_reorder(label, pct_below_lod), fill = file)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 50, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rep(okabe_ito, 2)) +
  labs(x = "% of measured participants below the limit of detection", y = NULL,
       fill = "data file",
       title = "Many exposure markers (VOCs, PFAS, metals) are mostly below the detection limit",
       subtitle = "only lab tests with at least one value below LOD are shown") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
```

What this looks like in the values themselves, for blood cadmium:

```{r fig-lod-cadmium, fig.height = 3.5}
nhanes_raw %>%
  filter(!is.na(LBXBCD)) %>%
  mutate(below_lod = factor(LBDBCDLC, levels = 0:1, labels = c("measured", "below LOD"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = LBXBCD, fill = below_lod)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(2, 6)]) +
  labs(x = "blood cadmium (\u00b5g/L, log scale)", y = "participants", fill = NULL,
       title = "All values below the LOD share one substitute value: a spike, not real variation")
```

# Distributions of the continuous measurements

From here on we look at **examined** participants only, because the others
have no exam or lab data.

```{r distribution-summary}
examined <- nhanes_raw %>% filter(RIDSTATR == 2)

skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) < 3 || sd(x) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}

continuous_vars <- var_info %>%
  filter(type_guess == "continuous / count", component %in% c("Examination", "Laboratory")) %>%
  pull(variable)

distribution_summary <- map_dfr(continuous_vars, function(v) {
  x <- examined[[v]]
  tibble(variable = v, n = sum(!is.na(x)),
         min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE), median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
         max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE), skewness = skewness(x))
}) %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, label), by = "variable")

length(continuous_vars)
sum(distribution_summary$skewness > 1, na.rm = TRUE)   # strongly right-skewed
sum(distribution_summary$min < 0)                      # impossible negative values?

distribution_summary %>% slice_max(skewness, n = 10) %>%
  select(variable, label, min, median, max, skewness) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r fig-skewness, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(distribution_summary, aes(skewness)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = okabe_ito[4]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = pseudo_log_trans(base = 10),
                     breaks = c(-10, -1, 0, 1, 10, 100)) +
  labs(x = "skewness (pseudo-log axis)", y = "number of variables",
       title = "Most continuous lab variables are strongly right-skewed (skewness > 1)")
```

Raw versus log-transformed distributions for a few key variables (examined
adults):

```{r fig-raw-vs-log, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 11}
key_vars <- c("BMXBMI", "LBXGH", "LBXHSCRP", "LBXCOT", "LBXSATSI", "LBXBPB")
key_labels <- var_info %>% filter(variable %in% key_vars) %>%
  mutate(facet = str_wrap(paste0(variable, ": ", label), 22)) %>%
  select(variable, facet)

key_long <- examined %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  select(all_of(key_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  filter(!is.na(value)) %>%
  left_join(key_labels, by = "variable")

p_raw <- ggplot(key_long, aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = okabe_ito[2]) +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "raw value", y = "participants")
p_log <- ggplot(key_long, aes(log10(value))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = okabe_ito[3]) +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "log10(value)", y = "participants")

p_raw / p_log +
  plot_annotation(title = "Log transformation makes most skewed variables roughly symmetric",
                  subtitle = paste("cotinine: spike = values below the LOD, then two groups (non-smokers vs. smokers);",
                                   "HbA1c keeps a right tail (diabetes range)")) &
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7))
```

Some variables are not skewed but **bimodal because of biology**, for example
testosterone, which differs by an order of magnitude between men and women:

```{r fig-testosterone, fig.height = 3.5}
examined %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20, !is.na(LBXTST)) %>%
  mutate(sex = factor(RIAGENDR, 1:2, c("Male", "Female"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = LBXTST, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6, colour = NA) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = okabe_ito[c(2, 1)]) +
  labs(x = "total testosterone (ng/dL, log scale)", y = "density", fill = NULL,
       title = "Testosterone: two populations, so analyses must account for sex")
```

# Outliers

Outliers are flagged with the box-plot (IQR) rule: below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or
above Q3 + 1.5·IQR. On skewed data this rule flags many values that are simply
the long tail of the distribution, so we compare the raw scale with the log
scale (variables with only positive values).

```{r outliers}
iqr_outlier_pct <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75)); iqr <- diff(q)
  100 * mean(x < q[1] - 1.5 * iqr | x > q[2] + 1.5 * iqr)
}

outlier_summary <- map_dfr(continuous_vars, function(v) {
  x <- examined[[v]]
  tibble(variable = v,
         pct_outlier_raw = iqr_outlier_pct(x),
         pct_outlier_log = if (min(x, na.rm = TRUE) > 0) iqr_outlier_pct(log10(x)) else NA_real_)
})

summarise(outlier_summary,
          median_pct_raw = median(pct_outlier_raw),
          median_pct_log = median(pct_outlier_log, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r fig-outliers, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 5.5}
ggplot(outlier_summary, aes(pct_outlier_raw, pct_outlier_log)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(colour = okabe_ito[4], alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "% flagged as outlier, raw scale", y = "% flagged, log10 scale",
       title = "Most 'outliers' disappear\nafter log transformation")
```

Plausibility check on a few clinical variables (examined adults): are there
values that are physiologically impossible rather than just extreme?

```{r plausibility}
examined %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  select(BMXBMI, BMXHT, BMXWT, BPXOSY1, BPXODI1, BPXOPLS1, LBXGH, LBXHGB) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(value)), min = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
            median = median(value, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

# Redundancy and correlation

## Unit duplicates are perfectly correlated

```{r duplicate-correlation}
duplicate_pairs <- var_info %>%
  filter(role %in% c("measurement", "unit duplicate"), file != "FASTQX_L") %>%
  group_by(file, base_label) %>% filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(primary = first(variable), duplicate = nth(variable, 2), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(correlation = map2_dbl(primary, duplicate,
                                ~ cor(nhanes_raw[[.x]], nhanes_raw[[.y]], use = "complete.obs")))

nrow(duplicate_pairs)
summary(duplicate_pairs$correlation)

# pairs that are not exactly 1 (rounding of low values in one of the two units)
duplicate_pairs %>% filter(correlation < 0.999)
```

## Correlation between key clinical variables

Spearman correlation (rank-based, so robust to skewness and outliers) between
key variables in examined adults, ordered by hierarchical clustering. The three
replicate blood-pressure readings are included on purpose.

```{r fig-correlation, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 9}
corr_vars <- c("RIDAGEYR", "INDFMPIR", "BMXWT", "BMXHT", "BMXBMI", "BMXWAIST", "BMXHIP",
               "BMXARMC", "BPXOSY1", "BPXOSY2", "BPXOSY3", "BPXODI1", "BPXOPLS1",
               "LBXGH", "LBXSGL", "LBDHDD", "LBXTC", "LBXSTR", "LBXHSCRP", "LBXWBCSI",
               "LBXHGB", "LBXPLTSI", "LBXCOT", "LBXSATSI", "LBXSASSI", "LBXSGTSI",
               "LBXSCR", "LBXSUA", "LBXVIDMS", "LBXBPB", "LBXBCD", "LBXSAL")

corr_mat <- examined %>%
  filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20) %>%
  select(all_of(corr_vars)) %>%
  cor(method = "spearman", use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

var_order <- rownames(corr_mat)[hclust(as.dist(1 - abs(corr_mat)))$order]

as_tibble(corr_mat, rownames = "var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "rho") %>%
  mutate(var1 = factor(var1, var_order), var2 = factor(var2, var_order)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(var1, var2, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = okabe_ito[4], mid = "white", high = okabe_ito[5],
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Spearman \u03c1",
       title = "Correlation structure of key variables (examined adults)",
       subtitle = "blocks: body size, blood pressure (3 replicate readings), liver enzymes, lipids") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

# Quality control with PCA: biology or technical factors?

To check whether participants group by biology or by a technical factor, we run
an **exploratory** PCA on examined adults. Two technical / design factors are
available: the six-month period of the examination (`RIDEXMON`, season) and
the examination session (`PHDSESNZ`; 0 = morning, 1 = afternoon/evening, which
also determines whether the participant was fasting).

Choices made only for this exploration (the final ones belong in the
preprocessing script):

* continuous exam and lab measurements with < 10 % missing in examined adults;
* complete cases only;
* log10 transformation of right-skewed variables (skewness > 1); a small offset
  (half the smallest positive value) is added when a variable contains zeros;
* standardisation (mean 0, SD 1) so that no variable dominates through its unit.

```{r pca}
adults_examined <- examined %>% filter(RIDAGEYR >= 20)

pca_vars <- continuous_vars[colMeans(is.na(adults_examined[continuous_vars])) < 0.10]

pca_input <- adults_examined %>%
  select(SEQN, RIDAGEYR, RIAGENDR, RIDEXMON, PHDSESNZ, all_of(pca_vars)) %>%
  drop_na(all_of(pca_vars))

log_if_skewed <- function(x) {
  if (skewness(x) <= 1 || min(x) < 0) return(x)
  offset <- if (min(x) == 0) min(x[x > 0]) / 2 else 0
  log10(x + offset)
}

pca_matrix <- pca_input %>% select(all_of(pca_vars)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), log_if_skewed)) %>%
  as.matrix()

pca <- prcomp(pca_matrix, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)

c(variables = length(pca_vars), participants = nrow(pca_input),
  dropped_incomplete = nrow(adults_examined) - nrow(pca_input))
```

```{r fig-pca-scree, fig.height = 3.5}
tibble(PC = seq_along(pca$sdev), var_explained = 100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(PC, var_explained)) +
  geom_col(fill = okabe_ito[4]) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "principal component", y = "% variance explained",
       title = "Scree plot: variance is spread over many components")
```

```{r fig-pca-scores, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 10}
var_pct <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1)

scores <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  bind_cols(pca_input %>% transmute(
    sex       = factor(RIAGENDR, 1:2, c("Male", "Female")),
    age_group = cut(RIDAGEYR, c(19, 39, 59, 80), labels = c("20-39", "40-59", "60-80")),
    period    = factor(RIDEXMON, 1:2, c("Nov-Apr", "May-Oct")),
    session   = factor(PHDSESNZ, 0:1, c("morning", "afternoon/evening"))
  ))

pca_panel <- function(colour_var, title) {
  ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = .data[[colour_var]])) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = okabe_ito, na.value = "grey70") +
    labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pct[1], " %)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pct[2], " %)"),
         colour = NULL, title = title) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1)))
}

(pca_panel("sex", "biology: sex") | pca_panel("age_group", "biology: age")) /
  (pca_panel("period", "technical: six-month period") |
     pca_panel("session", "technical: exam session")) +
  plot_annotation(title = "PCA of examined adults coloured by biological and technical factors")
```

Which variables drive the first two components?

```{r pca-loadings}
as_tibble(pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "variable") %>%
  pivot_longer(-variable, names_to = "PC", values_to = "loading") %>%
  group_by(PC) %>% slice_max(abs(loading), n = 8) %>% ungroup() %>%
  left_join(select(var_info, variable, label), by = "variable") %>%
  select(PC, variable, label, loading) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

# Summary: what the preprocessing script has to deal with

```{r summary-numbers, include = FALSE}
n_measurement  <- sum(var_info$role == "measurement")
n_not_examined <- sum(nhanes_raw$RIDSTATR == 1)
n_adults_exam  <- nrow(adults_examined)
n_dup          <- sum(var_info$role == "unit duplicate")
n_codes_vars   <- n_distinct(special_codes$variable)
n_lod_half     <- sum(lod_info$pct_below_lod > 50)
n_skewed       <- sum(distribution_summary$skewness > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

* **Variables.** Only `r n_measurement` of the 486 columns are candidate
  features; the others are the identifier, survey weights and design variables,
  comment codes and `r n_dup` unit duplicates (correlation ≈ 1, keep one of each).
* **Samples.** `r n_not_examined` participants were interviewed but never
  examined and have no exam or lab data; children have many adult measures
  missing by design. Most analyses will use the `r n_adults_exam` examined
  adults (≥ 20 y).
* **Missing data are structural, not random.** Missingness follows the study
  design (examination status, age, fasting and other subsamples). Variables
  measured only in a subsample must either be analysed within that subsample
  or left out; imputing them would invent data for people who were never
  eligible.
* **Disguised missing values.** `r n_codes_vars` variables contain codes for
  refused / don't know that must be recoded to `NA` (see table in section 5.1).
* **Top-coding.** Age (80) and income-to-poverty ratio (5) are capped.
* **Limit of detection.** `r n_lod_half` lab tests have more than half of the
  values below the LOD; these values are substitutes, not measurements (MNAR).
  Such variables carry little information as continuous features.
* **Skewness.** `r n_skewed` of `r length(continuous_vars)` continuous
  variables have skewness > 1: log transformation is needed before parametric
  tests, PCA or distance-based methods. Most IQR "outliers" are tail values of
  skewed distributions rather than errors.
* **Biology that must be modelled.** Strong sex differences (e.g.
  testosterone) and age effects: sex and age are natural adjustment variables.
* **Survey design.** NHANES is a weighted, stratified sample. Unweighted
  analyses describe this sample, not the US population (limitation to report).
